message.content:
The number of distinct legal positions that can arise in a game of chess is astronomically large.  In 1950 Claude Shannon famously estimated this number to be on the order of

\[
N_{\text{positions}} \;\approx\; 10^{43}
\]

This figure is often called the **Shannon number** and is widely cited as a lower bound for the true count.

More recent computational studies have refined the estimate.  Using exhaustive enumeration of all legal positions up to a certain depth, researchers have found that the total number of legal positions is roughly

\[
N_{\text{positions}} \;\approx\; 10^{46}
\]

(about 1 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000).

So, depending on whether you use the classic Shannon estimate or the more recent computational bounds, the total number of possible arrangements in a chess game lies somewhere between \(10^{43}\) and \(10^{46}\).
